searchDocs.title: Overview​
searchDocs.content: Nvidia graphics cards require proprietary drivers to unlock their full performance and features on Linux. The installation process varies between distributions, as each one manages proprietary packages and repositories differently.  This guide covers the installation of the Nvidia drivers on Debian, Fedora, and Arch Linux, including enabling the required repositories and installing the appropriate packages.

searchDocs.title: Debian​
searchDocs.content: Site: https://wiki.debian.org/NvidiaGraphicsDrivers  Add the contrib, non-free, and non-free-firmware components to the /etc/apt/sources.list file, as shown below. This example is for Debian 13 (Trixie):  deb http://deb.debian.org/debian/ trixie main contrib non-free non-free-firmware deb http://security.debian.org/debian-security/ trixie-security contrib non-free main non-free-firmware deb http://deb.debian.org/debian/ trixie-updates non-free-firmware non-free contrib main   Update the package lists:  sudo apt update -y   Install the Linux kernel headers:  sudo apt install linux-headers-generic   Install the Nvidia drivers:  sudo apt install nvidia-kernel-dkms nvidia-driver   Note: Installing nvidia-driver may not enable DLSS support. If you need it, install the full driver package instead:  sudo apt install nvidia-driver-full

searchDocs.title: Fedora​
searchDocs.content: Site: https://rpmfusion.org/  The Nvidia drivers are distributed through the RPM Fusion repositories. Add the free and nonfree repositories:  sudo dnf install https://download1.rpmfusion.org/free/fedora/rpmfusion-free-release-$(rpm -E %fedora).noarch.rpm sudo dnf install https://download1.rpmfusion.org/nonfree/fedora/rpmfusion-nonfree-release-$(rpm -E %fedora).noarch.rpm   Update the system:  sudo dnf update -y   Install the drivers:  sudo dnf install akmod-nvidia -y sudo dnf install xorg-x11-drv-nvidia-cuda -y

searchDocs.title: Arch Linux​
searchDocs.content: Wiki: https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/NVIDIA  The Nvidia driver can be selected during the installation process, which makes this step straightforward.

searchDocs.title: Overview​
searchDocs.content: Vim is a highly configurable text editor designed for efficient editing of plain‑text files. It runs in the terminal and provides powerful keyboard‑based navigation, extensibility through plugins, and support for many programming languages.

searchDocs.title: Installation​
searchDocs.content: The installation steps differ slightly between distributions. The commands below install the binary with clipboard support when available.

searchDocs.title: Fedora​
searchDocs.content: For a compiled build that supports the system clipboard, install vim-X11 (works on both X11 and Wayland):  sudo dnf install vim-X11   Note: The binary with clipboard support is named vimx. To check the clipboard support open vimx and run :echo has('clipboard'). It must return 1.

searchDocs.title: Dependencies for Plugin Manager and LSP Support​
searchDocs.content: Vim‑plug is a lightweight plugin manager, while coc.nvim provides language‑server integration. Install the required tools with:

searchDocs.title: Fedora​
searchDocs.content: sudo dnf install git nodejs npm

searchDocs.title: Installing vim‑plug​
searchDocs.content: Download the plug script into Vim’s autoload directory:  curl -fLo ~/.vim/autoload/plug.vim --create-dirs \ https://raw.githubusercontent.com/junegunn/vim-plug/master/plug.vim   Open Vim and run :PlugInstall to fetch the plugins listed in your .vimrc.  Tip: If you plan to use language‑server support, install the desired servers (e.g. clangd, pyright, rust-analyzer, fortls).

searchDocs.title: Key Features​
searchDocs.content: Software Rendering: Full CPU-based rendering engine for maximum portability.2D Primitives: Supports lines, filled triangles, rectangles, and circles.Sprite Management: High-level sprite loading (PAM format) and composition.Alpha Blending: Sophisticated alpha compositing for seamless sprite layering.Frame Buffer Control: Direct management of RGBA pixel buffers.Zero External Dependencies: Built using only the standard C library.PAM Export: Quick snapshots of the framebuffer in PAM (P7) format.

searchDocs.title: Core Data Structures​
searchDocs.content: The library relies on several fundamental types and structures to manage graphics data.

searchDocs.title: Primitive Types​
searchDocs.content: edl_u32: A 32-bit unsigned integer used for colors and dimensions.

searchDocs.title: Vectors​
searchDocs.content: EDL_VEC2: A 2D integer vector. x: The X-coordinate or width.y: The Y-coordinate or height.

searchDocs.title: Graphics Objects​
searchDocs.content: EDL_SCREEN: Represents the drawing canvas (framebuffer). res_x: Width of the screen in pixels.res_y: Height of the screen in pixels.buffer: Pointer to the 32-bit RGBA pixel buffer. EDL_SPRITE: Represents a graphical sprite. width: Width of the sprite in pixels.height: Height of the sprite in pixels.img: Pointer to the array containing the ARGB pixel data.

searchDocs.title: Color Management​
searchDocs.content: Colors in EDL are represented as 32-bit unsigned integers (edl_u32) in ARGB format. Each 8-bit segment represents a color component or the alpha (transparency) layer.

searchDocs.title: Color Format​
searchDocs.content: The byte order in memory is A | R | G | B (Alpha in the most significant byte).  Component	Bits	RangeAlpha	24-31	0-255 Red	16-23	0-255 Green	8-15	0-255 Blue	0-7	0-255  Hexadecimal Examples:  Red: 0xFFFF0000Green: 0xFF00FF00Blue: 0xFF0000FFBlack: 0xFF000000White: 0xFFFFFFFF

searchDocs.title: Color Conversion and Manipulation​
searchDocs.content: edl_from_hexa_to_rgba​  Converts a 32-bit hexadecimal color into individual 8-bit components.  Input: color (edl_u32)Output: r, g, b, a (unsigned char*)  Example bitmasking for Blue component:blue = color & 0xFF;  Example bitmasking for Alpha component:alpha = (color >> 24) & 0xFF;  edl_from_rgba_to_hexa​  Converts individual 8-bit RGBA components into a single 32-bit hexadecimal color.  Input: r, g, b, a (unsigned char)Output: color (edl_u32*)  edl_mix_color​  Performs alpha blending to mix a foreground color with a background color.  Input: cf (foreground), cb (background)Output: cp (resulting pixel color)

searchDocs.title: Return Status​
searchDocs.content: All functions return an int status code:  EDL_SUCCESS (0): The operation completed successfully.EDL_FAILURE (1): The operation failed (e.g., null pointer, allocation error, or I/O failure).

searchDocs.title: Screen Functions​
searchDocs.content: Function	Descriptionedl_init_screen	Allocates and initializes a framebuffer of specified resolution and color. edl_dalloc_screen	Frees the allocated framebuffer memory. edl_clear_screen	Fills the entire screen buffer with a solid color. edl_take_snapshot	Writes the current buffer to a sequentially named PAM file (e.g., output_0000.pam). edl_write_sprite_on_buffer	Renders a sprite onto the screen at a given position with alpha blending and clipping.

searchDocs.title: Sprite Functions​
searchDocs.content: Function	Descriptionedl_init_sprite	Initializes a sprite structure. edl_dalloc_sprite	Frees the sprite's image memory. edl_line_sprite	Generates a sprite containing a line between two points. edl_triangle_sprite	Generates a filled triangle using barycentric coordinates. edl_square_sprite	Generates a filled rectangle of specified dimensions. edl_circle_sprite	Generates a filled circle with a specified radius. edl_load_sprite	Loads sprite data from a PAM (P7) file.

searchDocs.title: Pixel Format & Exporting​
searchDocs.content: The library uses a 32-bit RGBA packed format. For file I/O, it utilizes the PAM (Portable AnyMap) format, which is highly efficient for raw pixel data.  Supported PAM Header:  P7 WIDTH <w> HEIGHT <h> DEPTH 4 MAXVAL 255 TUPLTYPE RGB_ALPHA ENDHDR <raw RGBA pixel data>

searchDocs.title: Implementation Example​
searchDocs.content: The following example demonstrates initializing a screen, creating a red square, and rendering it onto the screen.  #include "easydisplib.h" int main() { EDL_SCREEN screen; EDL_VEC2 res = {800, 600}; // Initialize a green screen if (edl_init_screen(&screen, res, 0xFF008800) != EDL_SUCCESS) { return 1; } // Create a red square sprite EDL_SPRITE square; edl_init_sprite(&square); edl_square_sprite(&square, 50, 50, 0x88FF0000); // Draw the sprite onto the screen at position (100, 200) EDL_VEC2 pos = {100, 200}; edl_write_sprite_on_buffer(&screen, &square, pos); // Export the frame as a PAM snapshot edl_take_snapshot(&screen); // Cleanup edl_dalloc_sprite(&square); edl_dalloc_screen(&screen); return 0; }

searchDocs.title: GTK 3.0: Dark theme​
searchDocs.content: Create the ~/.config/gtk-3.0 folder:  mkdir ~/.config/gtk-3.0   Move to the gtk-3.0 folder and create two files, bookmarks and settings.ini:  touch bookmarks touch settings.ini   Leave bookmarks empty and write the following in settings.ini:  [Settings] gtk-application-prefer-dark-theme=true

searchDocs.title: Wallpapers​
searchDocs.content: Create a folder to hold the wallpapers, if it does not exist yet. In this case, create ~/.config/wallpapers and save some wallpapers there:  mkdir ~/.config/wallpapers   If feh is not installed yet, install it:  Debian/Ubuntu:  sudo apt-get install feh   Fedora:  sudo dnf install feh   Arch:  sudo pacman -S feh   To set a wallpaper, run the following command:  feh --bg-scale ~/.config/wallpapers/name-wallpaper.jpg   To make it permanent in i3, add the following line to the i3 config file:  exec feh --bg-scale ~/.config/wallpapers/name-wallpaper.jpg   feh only sets fixed wallpapers, as the slideshow option does not work with the --bg-XX background options. To have a slideshow of wallpapers, the best option is to use systemd user services. The first step is to create the user folder that will hold the user services:  mkdir ~/.config/systemd/user/   Then create the wallpaper.service file inside the user services folder and paste the content below:  [Unit] Description=Set random wallpaper using feh [Service] Type=oneshot ExecStart=/usr/bin/feh --bg-scale --randomize -r %h/.config/wallpapers   Once the service is created, it is time to create the timer that will trigger it. In the same folder, create the wallpaper.timer file and paste the following content:  [Unit] Description=Set random wallpaper periodically [Timer] OnStartupSec=1sec OnUnitActiveSec=5min Unit=wallpaper.service [Install] WantedBy=timers.target   Finally, reload the user daemon to pick up the new services, then enable the timer and start the service:  systemctl --user daemon-reload systemctl --user enable wallpaper.timer systemctl --user start wallpaper.service   More information about systemd services for wallpaper slideshows can be found in the ihaveabackup.net blog post.

searchDocs.title: Picom​
searchDocs.content: Create the directory that will hold the Picom configuration file:  mkdir .config/picom touch .config/picom/picom.conf   Edit the picom.conf file and write the following:  backend = "glx"; # Use OpenGL to improve performance vsync = true; # This avoids tearing. glx-no-stencil = true; glx-no-rebind-pixmap = true; use-damage = true; # Other useful options refresh-rate = 0; # 0 = autodetect vsync-use-glfinish = false; unredir-if-possible = false; # This is important to vsync work correctly. # Transparencies (optional) shadow = false; fading = false;

searchDocs.title: Overview​
searchDocs.content: i3wm is a tiling window manager for X11, designed primarily for keyboard-driven workflows. It is lightweight, highly configurable, and fully controlled through plain-text configuration files.  This guide covers the installation of i3wm on Debian and the setup of its two main configuration files, i3 and i3status.  Site: https://i3wm.org/

searchDocs.title: Installation​
searchDocs.content: i3wm can be selected during the Arch Linux installation, and Fedora has its own i3 spin. For this reason, only the Debian installation is covered here. Before installing i3wm, it is necessary to install Xorg and a display manager. The command to install Xorg, SDDM and i3wm is:  sudo apt install xorg sddm i3

searchDocs.title: i3wm configuration​
searchDocs.content: The main configuration files are ~/.config/i3/config and ~/.config/i3status/config. A configuration example is provided below:

searchDocs.title: i3wm config file​
searchDocs.content: Open the file ~/.config/i3/config, clear its contents and paste the following:  # This file has been auto-generated by i3-config-wizard(1). # It will not be overwritten, so edit it as you like. # # Should you change your keyboard layout some time, delete # this file and re-run i3-config-wizard(1). # # i3 config file (v4) # # Please see https://i3wm.org/docs/userguide.html for a complete reference! set $mod Mod4 # Font for window titles. Will also be used by the bar unless a different font # is used in the bar {} block below. font pango:DaddyTimeMono Nerd Font 12 # This font is widely installed, provides lots of unicode glyphs, right-to-left # text rendering and scalability on retina/hidpi displays (thanks to pango). #font pango:DejaVu Sans Mono 8 # Start XDG autostart .desktop files using dex. See also # https://wiki.archlinux.org/index.php/XDG_Autostart exec --no-startup-id dex --autostart --environment i3 # The combination of xss-lock, nm-applet and pactl is a popular choice, so # they are included here as an example. Modify as you see fit. # xss-lock grabs a logind suspend inhibit lock and will use i3lock to lock the # screen before suspend. Use loginctl lock-session to lock your screen. exec --no-startup-id xss-lock --transfer-sleep-lock -- i3lock -c 000000 --nofork bindsym $mod+Mod1+l exec i3lock -c 000000 # NetworkManager is the most popular way to manage wireless networks on Linux, # and nm-applet is a desktop environment-independent system tray GUI for it. exec --no-startup-id nm-applet # Blueman for bluetooth exec --no-startup-id blueman-applet # Set resolution at start #exec xrandr --output HDMI-0 --primary --mode 1920x1080 --pos 0x0 --rotate normal --output DP-0 --mode 2560x1440 --rate 144 - #bindsym $mod+o exec xrandr --output eDP-1 --primary --mode 1920x1200 --pos 0x0 --rotate normal --output DP-1-0 --off --output DP-1-1 --off --output DP-1-2 --off --output DP-1-3 --off --output HDMI-1-0 --off --output DP-1-4 --off #bindsym $mod+Shift+o exec xrandr --output eDP-1 --primary --mode 1920x1200 --pos 0x0 --rotate normal --output DP-1-0 --off --output DP-1-1 --off --output DP-1-2 --off --output DP-1-3 --off --output HDMI-1-0 --mode 1920x1080 --pos 2560x204 --rotate normal --output DP-1-4 --off # Wallpaper # Fix Wallpaper. Not possible to use --slide-show property in feh when using --bg-XX for setting background. Only on window mode. exec feh --bg-scale ~/.config/wallpapers/name-of-wallpaper.png # Picom: compositor exec --no-startup-id picom --config ~/.config/picom/picom.conf # Use pactl to adjust volume in PulseAudio. set $refresh_i3status killall -SIGUSR1 i3status bindsym XF86AudioRaiseVolume exec --no-startup-id pactl set-sink-volume @DEFAULT_SINK@ +5% && $refresh_i3status bindsym XF86AudioLowerVolume exec --no-startup-id pactl set-sink-volume @DEFAULT_SINK@ -5% && $refresh_i3status bindsym XF86AudioMute exec --no-startup-id pactl set-sink-mute @DEFAULT_SINK@ toggle && $refresh_i3status bindsym XF86AudioMicMute exec --no-startup-id pactl set-source-mute @DEFAULT_SOURCE@ toggle && $refresh_i3status # Brightness #bindsym XF86MonBrightnessUp exec brightnessctl -d intel_backlight s +5% > /dev/null && notify-send Brightness $(($(brightnessctl get) * 10 / 937 * 10))% -h string:x-canonical-private-synchronous:brightness_percentage --app-name System #bindsym XF86MonBrightnessDown exec brightnessctl -d intel_backlight s 5%- > /dev/null && notify-send Brightness $(($(brightnessctl get) * 10 / 937 * 10))% -h string:x-canonical-private-synchronous:brightness_percentage --app-name System # Use Mouse+$mod to drag floating windows to their wanted position floating_modifier $mod # move tiling windows via drag & drop by left-clicking into the title bar, # or left-clicking anywhere into the window while holding the floating modifier. tiling_drag modifier titlebar # start a terminal #bindsym $mod+Return exec i3-sensible-terminal bindsym $mod+Return exec alacritty # kill focused window bindsym $mod+Shift+q kill # start dmenu (a program launcher) bindsym $mod+d exec --no-startup-id dmenu_run -fn 'DaddyTimeMono Nerd Font:regular:pixelsize=20' # A more modern dmenu replacement is rofi: # bindcode $mod+40 exec "rofi -modi drun,run -show drun" # There also is i3-dmenu-desktop which only displays applications shipping a # .desktop file. searchDocs.title: Raspberry Pi OS​
searchDocs.content: The fastest way is to download the Raspberry Pi Imager and follow the instructions to install the Lite version of the Raspberry Pi OS, which has no Desktop Environment installed. The system has to be installed on an SD card. Once the process is finished, insert the SD card into the slot on the Raspberry Pi so the system can be loaded for the first time. After the first boot, update and upgrade the system.  sudo apt-get update -y sudo apt-get upgrade -y

searchDocs.title: Enable SSH​
searchDocs.content: Enabling SSH is useful to configure the Raspberry Pi remotely. The SSH connection is enabled through the Raspberry Pi configuration.  sudo raspi-config   Then select the third option, Interface Options, and I1 SSH to enable it. Once it is enabled, it is possible to connect from another computer on the same network by running the following command:  ssh <pi-username>@<ip-raspberry>   Example:  Pi username: NasPiPi IP address: 192.168.1.23  ssh NasPi@192.168.1.23   Note: After entering the credentials, it will ask for a password.

searchDocs.title: Setting up a static IP​
searchDocs.content: The static IP is set up through the Network Manager application. The first step is to identify the connection and save its name.  nmcli connection show   This will show something like this:  NAME UUID TYPE DEVICE Wired connection 1 4b3b674a-d346-5cfa-3b30-df70e6db4b81 ethernet eth0   Then modify the connection:  nmcli connection modify "Wired connection 1" \ ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.78/24 \ ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 \ ipv4.method manual   After this command the IP of the Raspberry Pi is set to 192.168.1.78, and the change is persistent.

searchDocs.title: RAID 1 storage​
searchDocs.content: There are different types of RAID storage. RAID 1 consists of creating a mirror of a set of data on two or more disks. For the purpose of a home NAS, using two disks in a RAID 1 configuration is enough, although this is something to evaluate in each case.  To create the RAID 1 virtual disk, the mdadm program has to be installed:  sudo apt install mdadm   The next step is to list the disks:  lsblk   Here is an example of the output:  NAME MAJ:MIN RM SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINTS loop0 7:0 0 2G 0 loop sda 8:0 0 3.6T 0 disk └─sda1 8:1 0 3.6T 0 part sdc 8:32 0 3.6T 0 disk └─sdc1 8:33 0 3.6T 0 part zram0 253:0 0 2G 0 disk [SWAP] nvme0n1 259:0 0 238.5G 0 disk ├─nvme0n1p1 259:1 0 512M 0 part /boot/firmware └─nvme0n1p2 259:2 0 238G 0 part /   In this case, the two disks of 3.6TB are sda and sdc. To create the device associated with the RAID, the following command is used:  sudo mdadm --create /dev/md0 \ --level=1 \ --raid-devices=2 \ /dev/sda /dev/sdc   If the disks are listed again, the device md0 will appear:  NAME MAJ:MIN RM SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINTS loop0 7:0 0 2G 0 loop sda 8:0 0 3.6T 0 disk └─sda1 8:1 0 3.6T 0 part └─md0 9:0 0 3.6T 0 raid1 /mnt/raid1 sdc 8:32 0 3.6T 0 disk └─sdc1 8:33 0 3.6T 0 part zram0 253:0 0 2G 0 disk [SWAP] nvme0n1 259:0 0 238.5G 0 disk ├─nvme0n1p1 259:1 0 512M 0 part /boot/firmware └─nvme0n1p2 259:2 0 238G 0 part /   Then format the file system to EXT4:  sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/md0   Finally, create a mount point for the device:  sudo mkdir /mnt/raid1 sudo mount /dev/md0 /mnt/raid1   To make the mount point permanent, find the UUID of the device md0. Run the following command and save the returned value:  sudo blkid /dev/md0   Then edit the file /etc/fstab and add the following line:  proc /proc proc defaults 0 0 ... UUID=4b3b674a-d346-5cfa-2f40-ef70e6db4c94 /mnt/raid1 ext4 defaults,nofail 0 0 ...   Finally, save the RAID configuration to mdadm.conf:  sudo mdadm --detail --scan | sudo tee -a /etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf   The last step is to update initramfs and reboot the system:  sudo update-initramfs -u reboot

searchDocs.title: Configure SMB​
searchDocs.content: Install Samba:  sudo apt update sudo apt install samba samba-common-bin

searchDocs.title: Create system users​
searchDocs.content: Samba users must first exist as system users. These users do not need a home directory, and their login can be disabled:  sudo adduser --no-create-home --disabled-login user1 sudo adduser --no-create-home --disabled-login user2   The creation and activation of a Samba user linked to the system user can be done by running the following commands:  sudo smbpasswd -a userX sudo smbpasswd -e userX   Then edit the file /etc/samba/smb.conf and add the shares like this:  [user1] path = /mnt/raid1 browseable = yes read only = no valid users = user1 [user2] path = /mnt/raid1 browseable = yes read only = no valid users = user2

searchDocs.title: Force the use of the SMB3 protocol​
searchDocs.content: In the same file, under the [global] section, add the following lines:  [global] ... ## Force Samba SMB3 protocol ## client min protocol = SMB3 server min protocol = SMB3 ...

searchDocs.title: Restart the Samba service​
searchDocs.content: sudo systemctl restart smbd

searchDocs.title: Reboot the system​
searchDocs.content: sudo reboot

searchDocs.title: Overview​
searchDocs.content: Fedora Sway is the official Fedora spin featuring the Sway window manager, an i3-compatible tiling window manager built for Wayland. It provides a minimal, keyboard-driven desktop environment that is highly customizable through its configuration files.  This guide covers the installation of Fedora Sway from a bootable image and the initial configuration of a fresh installation, including:  Setting up the Sway and Waybar configuration files. Updating the system and installing basic tools. Enabling Nvidia graphics card support. Site: https://fedoraproject.org/spins/sway/ Wiki: https://fedoraproject.org/wiki/Fedora_Project_Wiki

searchDocs.title: Installation​
searchDocs.content: Download the ISO image from the Fedora Sway spin page and create a bootable USB drive.Insert the bootable USB drive and boot the live environment.Press Super+Enter to open a terminal. Note that on Windows keyboards, the Super key corresponds to the Windows key.Run liveinst in the terminal to launch the installer.Follow the on-screen instructions and select the options that best fit your needs.  Once these steps are completed, the installation is finished.

searchDocs.title: Configuration files​
searchDocs.content: Sway configuration file​  Create an empty file called config inside the directory ~/.config/sway.  mkdir -p ~/.config/sway touch ~/.config/sway/config   You can use the configuration below (note that it assumes a Spanish keyboard layout), your own configuration, or copy the system default from /etc/sway/config.  To use this configuration, edit the file ~/.config/sway/config. Since this is a fresh install, Fedora Sway only includes the Nano text editor, which is the one used throughout this guide. Paste the following content:  # Default config for sway # # Copy this to ~/.config/sway/config and edit it to your liking. # # Read `man 5 sway` for a complete reference. ### Variables # # Logo key. Use Mod1 for Alt. set $mod Mod4 # Home row direction keys, like vim set $left h set $down j set $up k set $right l # Your preferred terminal emulator # Recommends: foot set $term alacritty # Your preferred application launcher # Note: pass the final command to swaymsg so that the resulting window can be opened # on the original workspace that the command was run on. # Recommends: rofi-wayland set $rofi_cmd rofi \ -terminal '$term' # Shows a combined list of the applications with desktop files and # executables from PATH. # TODO: add window with the next release of rofi-wayland set $menu $rofi_cmd -show combi -combi-modes drun#run -modes combi ### Output configuration # # Default wallpaper (more resolutions are available in /usr/share/backgrounds/sway/) # Requires: desktop-backgrounds-compat, swaybg, jxl-pixbuf-loader #output * bg /usr/share/backgrounds/default.jxl fill output * bg ~/Pictures/Wallpapers/orion-nebula.jpg fill # Example configuration: # # output HDMI-A-1 resolution 1920x1080 position 1920,0 # # You can get the names of your outputs by running: swaymsg -t get_outputs output HDMI-A-1 resolution 2560x1440 position 0,0 scale 1.25 output DP-1 resolution 1920x1080 position 2560,0 scale 1.0 exec_always --no-startup-id swaymsg "workspace 1, move workspace to output HDMI-A-1" exec_always --no-startup-id swaymsg "workspace 2, move workspace to output DP-1" ### Idle configuration # # Example configuration: # exec swayidle -w \ timeout 300 'swaylock -f -c 000000 -i ~/Pictures/Wallpapers/Moon.png' \ timeout 600 'swaymsg "output * power off"' resume 'swaymsg "output * power on"' \ before-sleep 'swaylock -f -c 000000 -i ~/Pictures/Wallpapers/Moon.png' # This will lock your screen after 300 seconds of inactivity, then turn off # your displays after another 300 seconds, and turn your screens back on when # resumed. It will also lock your screen before your computer goes to sleep. ### Input configuration # # Example configuration: # # input "2:14:SynPS/2_Synaptics_TouchPad" { # dwt enabled # tap enabled # natural_scroll enabled # middle_emulation enabled # } # # You can get the names of your inputs by running: swaymsg -t get_inputs # Read `man 5 sway-input` for more information about this section. input "type:keyboard" { xkb_layout "es" } ### Dark mode exec gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.interface color-scheme 'prefer-dark' exec gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.interface gtk-theme 'Adwaita-dark' exec gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.interface icon-theme 'breeze-dark' ### Key bindings # # Basics: # # Start a terminal bindsym $mod+Return exec $term # Kill focused window bindsym $mod+Shift+q kill # Start your launcher bindsym $mod+d exec $menu # Drag floating windows by holding down $mod and left mouse button. # Resize them with right mouse button + $mod. # Despite the name, also works for non-floating windows. # Change normal to inverse to use left mouse button for resizing and right # mouse button for dragging. floating_modifier $mod normal # Reload the configuration file bindsym $mod+Shift+c reload # Exit sway (logs you out of your Wayland session) bindsym $mod+Shift+e exec swaynag -t warning -m 'You pressed the exit shortcut. Do you really want to exit sway? This will end your Wayland session.' -B 'Yes, exit sway' 'swaymsg exit' # # Moving around: # # Move your focus around bindsym $mod+$left focus left bindsym $mod+$down focus down bindsym $mod+$up focus up bindsym $mod+$right focus right # Or use $mod+[up|down|left|right] bindsym $mod+Left focus left bindsym $mod+Down focus down bindsym $mod+Up focus up bindsym $mod+Right focus right # Move the focused window with the same, but add Shift bindsym $mod+Shift+$left move left bindsym $mod+Shift+$down move down bindsym $mod+Shift+$up move up bindsym $mod+Shift+$right move right # Ditto, with arrow keys bindsym $mod+Shift+Left move left bindsym $mod+Shift+Down move down bindsym $mod+Shift+Up move up bindsym $mod+Shift+Right move right # # Workspaces: # # Switch to workspace bindsym $mod+1 workspace number 1 bindsym $mod+2 workspace number 2 bindsym $mod+3 workspace number 3 bindsym $mod+4 workspace number 4 bindsym $mod+5 workspace number 5 bindsym $mod+6 workspace number 6 bindsym $mod+7 workspace number 7 bindsym $mod+8 workspace number 8 bindsym $mod+9 workspace number 9 bindsym $mod+0 workspace number 10 # Move focused container to workspace bindsym $mod+Shift+1 move container to workspace number 1 bindsym $mod+Shift+2 move container to workspace number 2 bindsym $mod+Shift+3 move container to workspace number 3 bindsym $mod+Shift+4 move container to workspace number 4 bindsym $mod+Shift+5 move container to workspace number 5 bindsym $mod+Shift+6 move container to workspace number 6 bindsym $mod+Shift+7 move container to workspace number 7 bindsym $mod+Shift+8 move container to workspace number 8 bindsym $mod+Shift+9 move container to workspace number 9 bindsym $mod+Shift+0 move container to workspace number 10 # Note: workspaces can have any name you want, not just numbers. # We just use 1-10 as the default. # # Layout stuff: # # You can "split" the current object of your focus with # $mod+b or $mod+v, for horizontal and vertical splits # respectively. bindsym $mod+b splith bindsym $mod+v splitv # Switch the current container between different layout styles bindsym $mod+s layout stacking bindsym $mod+w layout tabbed bindsym $mod+e layout toggle split # Make the current focus fullscreen bindsym $mod+f fullscreen # Toggle the current focus between tiling and floating mode bindsym $mod+Shift+space floating toggle # Swap focus between the tiling area and the floating area bindsym $mod+space focus mode_toggle # Move focus to the parent container bindsym $mod+a focus parent # # Scratchpad: # # Sway has a "scratchpad", which is a bag of holding for windows. # You can send windows there and get them back later. # Move the currently focused window to the scratchpad bindsym $mod+Shift+minus move scratchpad # Show the next scratchpad window or hide the focused scratchpad window. # If there are multiple scratchpad windows, this command cycles through them. bindsym $mod+minus scratchpad show # # Resizing containers: # mode "resize" { # left will shrink the containers width # right will grow the containers width # up will shrink the containers height # down will grow the containers height bindsym $left resize shrink width 10px bindsym $down resize grow height 10px bindsym $up resize shrink height 10px bindsym $right resize grow width 10px # Ditto, with arrow keys bindsym Left resize shrink width 10px bindsym Down resize grow height 10px bindsym Up resize shrink height 10px bindsym Right resize grow width 10px # Return to default mode bindsym Return mode "default" bindsym Escape mode "default" } bindsym $mod+r mode "resize" ### Lock screen bindsym Ctrl+Alt+l exec swaylock -f -e -c 000000 -i ~/Pictures/Wallpapers/Moon.png ### Power off and reboot bindsym Ctrl+Alt+r exec reboot bindsym Ctrl+Alt+p exec poweroff # Include configs from 3 locations: # - /usr/share/sway/config.d # - /etc/sway/config.d # - $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/sway/config.d ($HOME/.config/sway/config.d) # # If multiple directories contain the files with the same name, the later # directory takes precedence; `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/sway/config.d/20-swayidle.conf` # will always be loaded instead of `/usr/share/sway/config.d/20-swayidle.conf` # or `/etc/sway/config.d/20-swayidle.conf` # # This mechanism permits overriding our default configuration per-system # (/etc) or per-user ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME) basis. Just create the file you # want to modify/override in the higher-level directory. # # For example, to disable the default bar from Fedora configs, you'll need to # $ echo -n > "$HOME/.config/sway/config.d/90-bar.conf" # # Note the quoting, the $() and the arguments quoting. All the parts are equally # important to make the magic work. And if you want to learn the secret behind # the trick, it's all in the `wordexp(3)`. # include '$(/usr/libexec/sway/layered-include "/usr/share/sway/config.d/*.conf" "/etc/sway/config.d/*.conf" "${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/sway/config.d/*.conf")'   Note: This configuration will not work out of the box. It references custom wallpaper files and output names, and it sets Alacritty as the terminal, which is not installed yet (Fedora Sway uses Foot by default). searchDocs.content: Fedora groups related packages into installable sets, known as package groups. To list the available groups, run the following command:  dnf group list   The most relevant groups are:  sudo dnf group install development-tools sudo dnf group install c-development

searchDocs.title: Install graphic card drivers​
searchDocs.content: Nvidia​  Sway is a Wayland window manager and does not always work well with Nvidia hardware. In this case, installing the Nvidia drivers caused the system to crash repeatedly. The solution was to replace the default display manager, SDDM, with LightDM, and to modify the /usr/share/wayland-sessions/sway.desktop file.  1. Replace SDDM with LightDM  sudo dnf install lightdm lightdm-gtk sudo systemctl disable sddm.service sudo systemctl enable lightdm.service   2. Modify the sway.desktop file  Add the --unsupported-gpu flag to the /usr/share/wayland-sessions/sway.desktop file.  [Desktop Entry] Name=Sway Comment=An i3-compatible Wayland compositor Exec=start-sway --unsupported-gpu Type=Application DesktopNames=sway   After those two steps, the Nvidia drivers can be installed as described in the Nvidia drivers section.  Important: Reboot the system for the changes to take effect.
